1.note: See how you translated the phrase “And it happened” in 2:39, where it similarly introduces a new event.

The author is using one person who was involved, Solomon, to mean everyone who was involved in building these structures. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, as the UST does. See how you translated similar expressions throughout chapters 5, 6, and 7. Alternate translation: [when Solomon’s workers finished building]
See how you translated the similar expression in [3:1](ta:03). Alternate translation: [the temple of]
See how you translated the similar expression in [7:1](ta:07). Alternate translation: [his royal palace]

1.q: וְ⁠אֵת֙ כָּל־חֵ֣שֶׁק שְׁלֹמֹ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר חָפֵ֖ץ לַ⁠עֲשֽׂוֹת
1.note: The author is using Solomon’s **desire** to build further structures to represent those structures themselves. (He describes them in 9:15 and, with a further reference to desire, in 9:17–19.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and all of the other structures that Solomon delighted to build]

2.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **second**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [again] or [once more]

3.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 5:8. Alternate translation: [I have answered]

Yahweh is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [and the supplication that you made]
Here, **to my face** represents “in my presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in my presence]

See how you translated the similar expression in 3:2 and the similar expressions throughout chapter 8. Alternate translation: [for it to be a place where people will worship me] or [for it to be a place where my reputation will be made known]

Yahweh is responding to Solomon’s request in 8:29 “that your eyes may be opened to this house.” Solomon was speaking as if he wanted Yahweh always to be looking at the temple, but he meant that he wanted Yahweh always to be listening to the prayers that people offered toward the temple. Yahweh is saying that he will do this and, in addition, he will always care about the temple, the worship in it, and the prayers that people pray toward it. Yahweh is using his **heart** to represent his feelings and commitment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will always listen to the prayers that people pray toward the temple, and it will always be precious to me]
Yahweh is using the term **days** to refer to time, since time consists of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all the time]

4.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you walk** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Solomon, for his part (just as his father had done for his own part), is to live in the way that he describes. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. See how you translated the similar expression “you, you swore” in 1:17. Alternate translation: [And if you, for your part, walk] or [And if you personally walk]

4.q: אִם־תֵּלֵ֣ךְ לְ⁠פָנַ֗⁠י כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר הָלַ֜ךְ דָּוִ֤ד אָבִ֨י⁠ךָ֙ בְּ⁠תָם־לֵבָ֣ב וּ⁠בְ⁠יֹ֔שֶׁר
4.note: See how you translated the similar phrase in 3:6, where Solomon says to Yahweh about his father David, “he walked to your face in faithfulness and in righteousness and in uprightness of heart.” Alternate translation: [if you conduct yourself in my presence just as David your father conducted himself, with integrity in your motives and intentions and with upright actions]

The terms **statutes** and **judgments** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [if you obey all of my commandments]

5.note: Yahweh is speaking as if he would physically **raise up** the **throne** of Solomon to a high position above Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express his meaning using an equivalent expression or plain language. If you have already translated the book of 2 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 2 Samuel 3:10. Alternate translation: [then I will establish your rule over the kingdom of Israel]

5.q: אָבִ֨י⁠ךָ֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר לֹֽא־יִכָּרֵ֤ת לְ⁠ךָ֙ אִ֔ישׁ מֵ⁠עַ֖ל כִּסֵּ֥א יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
5.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [your father when I told him that a man to him would not be cut off from upon the throne of Israel]

5.q: לֹֽא־יִכָּרֵ֤ת לְ⁠ךָ֙ אִ֔ישׁ מֵ⁠עַ֖ל כִּסֵּ֥א יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
5.note: See how you translated this same sentence in 3:4. Alternate translation: [One of your descendants will always be the king of Israel]

6.note: Yahweh is speaking as if Solomon or his descendants would be walking behind him but then might **turn** away to walk in a different direction. He means that they would stop living in the manner in which he wants people to live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [If you or your sons ever stop following me] or [If you or your sons ever stop being devoted to me as your God]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **turn** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [If you ever turn]

6.q: תְּשֻׁב֜וּ⁠ן אַתֶּ֤ם & וְ⁠לֹ֤א תִשְׁמְרוּ֙ & לִ⁠פְנֵי⁠כֶ֑ם וַ⁠הֲלַכְתֶּ֗ם
6.note: The word **you** is singular in the first two instances because Yahweh is using it to refer to Solomon. The words **you** and **your** (and the implied “you” in the verbs **serve** and **bow down**) are plural in the rest of the verse because Yahweh is using them to refer to Solomon and his **sons**. Use the appropriate singular and plural forms in each case in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
Here, **to your faces** means “in front of you.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I have set in front of you]

Yahweh is speaking as if his commandments and statutes were objects that he had physically placed in front of the Israelites where they could see them. He means that he has given them these laws to obey. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have told you to obey]

In describing this possible condition, Yahweh is not envisioning that Solomon or later kings would **go** somewhere in order to **serve other gods and bow down to them**. He is using the term **go** to mean that a king might resolve to do these things and take action to do them (leading his Israelite subjects to do the same). Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. If you have already translated the book of 2 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 2 Samuel 7:3. Alternate translation: [and you decide to serve other gods and bow down to them]

When applied to “other gods,” the term “serve” refers to honoring them by living as their followers did, building shrines for them, and following religious practices such as praying to them and offering sacrifices to them. Bowing down to these gods (physically bowing to an idol that represented them in a shrine or temple) was a symbolic action of surrender to them as one’s lord. It represented a definitive further step, beyond the idea of “serving” or honoring them, that would provoke Yahweh’s judgment, as he describes in the following verses. So we recommend that you do not combine these two phrases in your translation. While their meaning is similar, there is a significant difference between them. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain in the text of your translation or in a footnote the significance of bowing down. Alternate translation: [and honor other gods and ultimately commit yourself to them by bowing down to them]

7.q: וְ⁠הִכְרַתִּ֣י אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל מֵ⁠עַ֨ל פְּנֵ֤י הָ⁠אֲדָמָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נָתַ֣תִּי לָ⁠הֶ֔ם
7.note: See how you translated the term “face” in 8:40. Alternate translation: [then I will cut off Israel from upon the surface of the ground that I have given to them]

7.q: וְ⁠הִכְרַתִּ֣י אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל מֵ⁠עַ֨ל פְּנֵ֤י הָ⁠אֲדָמָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נָתַ֣תִּי לָ⁠הֶ֔ם
7.note: See how you translated the term “Israel” in 4:20. Alternate translation: [then I will cut off the Israelites from upon the surface of the ground that I have given to them]

7.q: וְ⁠הִכְרַתִּ֣י אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל מֵ⁠עַ֨ל פְּנֵ֤י הָ⁠אֲדָמָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נָתַ֣תִּי לָ⁠הֶ֔ם
7.note: Yahweh is speaking as if he were actually going to **cut off** the Israelites **from … the ground**, as if they were a plant that he would remove from the ground with a sharp tool. He means that he will remove the Israelites from the land so that they will no longer live in it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [then I will remove the Israelites so that they will no longer live in the land that I have given to them]

Here, **before my face** represents “in front of me.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will send away from in front of me]

Yahweh is speaking as if the temple were actually a person whom he could **send away** with a command. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will destroy so that it no longer exists]

The word translated as **proverb** indicates in this context that people would use the specific case of Israel as a reference point for a general observation. The word translated as **taunt** means that people would use a comparison with what happened to Israel to mock or ridicule others who suffered a similar fate. So while the meaning of these terms is similar, there is a significant difference between them, and we recommend that you do not combine them into a single term or phrase in your translation. The UST models one way to show their different meanings.

8.note: This could mean: (1) that the author is leaving out a word that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. The parallel passage in 2 Chronicles 7:21 includes the word “which.” You could supply it in your translation if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And this temple, which is exalted] or [And although this temple is now exalted] or (2) that the author is saying that the temple will be **exalted** in the sense of lifted up or heaped up as a ruin. Alternate translation: [And this temple will become a heap of ruins]

The expression **will be astonished** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [what has happened to it will astonish everyone passing by it, and they will hiss]

To **hiss** was to make a sound like a snake by forcing breath through one’s teeth. In this culture, hissing was a way of expressing derision and contempt, like booing or whistling in some modern cultures. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and will hiss in derision]

8.q: וְ⁠אָמְר֗וּ עַל־מֶ֨ה עָשָׂ֤ה יְהוָה֙ כָּ֔כָה לָ⁠אָ֥רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֖את וְ⁠לַ⁠בַּ֥יִת הַ⁠זֶּֽה
8.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And they will ask why Yahweh did this to this land and to this temple]

The author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense here, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And people will ask]

9.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And they will say that it was because]
The author is continuing to use the pronoun **they** in a general sense. Alternate translation: [And others will answer]

The people are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh did this because]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:21. Alternate translation: [their ancestors]

The people Yahweh is envisioning are speaking here as if the Israelites were physically holding onto **other gods** with their hands. They mean that they became devoted to or loyal to these gods. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they embraced other gods] or [and they became loyal to other gods]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **served them** before the information about **bowed down to them**, as in 9:6. Alternate translation: [and served them and bowed down to them]

9.q: הֵבִ֤יא יְהוָה֙ עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֔ם אֵ֥ת כָּל־הָ⁠רָעָ֖ה הַ⁠זֹּֽאת
9.note: The author is speaking here as if Yahweh had actually **brought** harm to the people, as if he had carried it over and set it down upon them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh caused all of this harm to happen to them]

10.note: See how you translated the similar expression in [9:1](ta:09). Alternate translation: [the temple of Yahweh and his royal palace]

11.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **delight**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in keeping with everything he wanted]

12.note: The author is using **they were not right in his eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they were not acceptable in his judgment” or “they were not satisfactory in his opinion.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but in his judgment, they were not an appropriate gift]

13.q: מָ֚ה הֶ⁠עָרִ֣ים הָ⁠אֵ֔לֶּה אֲשֶׁר־נָתַ֥תָּה לִּ֖⁠י אָחִ֑⁠י
13.note: Hiram was using the question form to express his dissatisfaction with the cities that Solomon had given him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I do not like these cities that you have given to me, my brother!]

Hiram is speaking here as if he and Solomon were actually **brothers**. Hiram means that he and Solomon are allies or fellow kings who have a close relationship. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my fellow king] or [my ally]

It is no longer clear what the term **Cabul** means. Some interpreters suggest that the context indicates that it means “worthless” or “good for nothing.” But since this is uncertain, we recommend that you simply use the name in your translation without explaining its meaning, and that you let readers infer the meaning from the context.

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and that is still their name to this day]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:8. Alternate translation: [right up to the time of this writing]

14.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֥ח חִירָ֖ם לַ⁠מֶּ֑לֶךְ מֵאָ֥ה וְ⁠עֶשְׂרִ֖ים כִּכַּ֥ר זָהָֽב
14.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand how much Hiram had done for Solomon and why he was therefore so disappointed to receive what he felt was a paltry acknowledgement of his contributions. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

These 120 **kikkars of gold** weighed a total of about 4,000 kilograms or about 9,000 pounds. In your translation, you could use the ancient measurement and spell the word “kikkar” the way it sounds in your language. You could also use the metric measurement given in the UST or use the measurement that your language and culture customarily use. Alternatively, you could use the ancient measurement and put a modern measurement in parentheses in the text or in a footnote.

15.note: The author is using this phrase to introduce a new topic related to the reign of Solomon, which he has been describing in the course of the story he is telling about the kings of Israel. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new topic.
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:13. Alternate translation: [the levy that King Solomon raised] or [the work force that King Solomon called up]

The word **Millo** is the name of a place. It was likely a raised platform or landfill that formed part of Jerusalem’s fortifications. If you have already translated the book of 2 Samuel, see how you translated this name in 2 Samuel 5:9.

16.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:25. Alternate translation: [had gone]

It might seem that the expression **burned it with fire** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and he had burned it down]

The author is not referring to a specific **Canaanite**. He means all of the Canaanites who lived in Gezer. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Canaanites who lived in that city]

A **dowry** is a payment or transfer of money, property, or valuable goods by a woman’s family to her new husband or his family at the time of their marriage. Typically in the biblical culture, a man would instead pay a bride-price to the woman’s family. But some men, especially rulers such as Pharaoh, gave property or territory to their daughters when they were married. If your readers would not be familiar with what a dowry is, you could explain it in your translation with a general term or a descriptive phrase. Alternate translation: [as a gift to his daughter on the occasion of her marriage to Solomon]

18.note: The author assumes that readers will understand that by **the land**, he means the land of Judah. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the land of Judah]

19.q: וְ⁠אֵ֣ת ׀ חֵ֣שֶׁק שְׁלֹמֹ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֤ר חָשַׁק֙ לִ⁠בְנ֤וֹת
19.note: See how you translated the similar expression in [9:1](ta:09). Alternate translation: [and all of the other structures that Solomon desired to build]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **dominion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and in the entire territory that he ruled]

20.note: The expression **the ones being left** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the ones remaining]

The author is not referring to a specific **Amorite** or to specific members of any of these other people groups. He means those people groups in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites]
See how you translated the similar expression in [6:1](ta:06). Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

21.note: The masculine term **sons** has a generic sense here that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [their descendants]

It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [whom the sons of Israel were not able to devote]

The word that the ULT translates as **devote** describes the cultural practice of giving something over to Yahweh so that humans will no longer be able to use it. If you have already translated the book of Joshua, see how you translated this term in its frequent occurrences there. In this context, the term means to “destroy completely.” Alternate translation: [to destroy completely]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:13. Alternate translation: [Solomon called them up as a work force]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they still serve as forced labor to this day]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:8. Alternate translation: [right up to the time of this writing]

22.note: In the first instance, the term **servant** describes in this context a forced laborer. In the second instance, the term **servants** refers to royal officials, as in 1:2 and often elsewhere in this book. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [a forced laborer … his royal officials]

23.q: אֵ֣לֶּה ׀ שָׂרֵ֣י הַ⁠נִּצָּבִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֤ר עַל־הַ⁠מְּלָאכָה֙ לִ⁠שְׁלֹמֹ֔ה חֲמִשִּׁ֖ים וַ⁠חֲמֵ֣שׁ מֵא֑וֹת הָ⁠רֹדִ֣ים בָּ⁠עָ֔ם הָ⁠עֹשִׂ֖ים בַּ⁠מְּלָאכָֽה
23.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that there were **550** commanders before the information about what the commanders did. Alternate translation: [There were 550 commanders of the deputies who were over the work for Solomon, the ones ruling over the people doing the work]

25.q: וְ⁠הֶעֱלָ֣ה שְׁלֹמֹ֡ה & עֹל֣וֹת וּ⁠שְׁלָמִ֗ים עַל־הַ⁠מִּזְבֵּ֨חַ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בָּנָ֣ה לַ⁠יהוָ֔ה וְ⁠הַקְטֵ֣יר אִתּ֔⁠וֹ אֲשֶׁ֖ר לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה
25.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the **incense** with the information about the **burnt offerings and peace offerings**. Alternate translation: [Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and he burned incense with it on the altar that he had built for Yahweh, which was to the face of Yahweh]
The pronoun **it** refers to the offerings that Solomon made. It may be more natural in your language to use a plural pronoun. Alternate translation: [with them]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:64. Alternate translation: [which was in front of Yahweh’s temple]

The term translated as **completed** here is different from the term translated as “finished” in [9:1](ta:09). The author is not restating that Solomon had finished building the temple, even though he is concluding this account of Solomon’s building projects, and he often concludes an account with a review statement. Instead, he means that by offering these sacrifices on the occasions of Israel’s three great annual feasts, Solomon made the Jerusalem temple the center of Israel’s worship. The Israelites no longer worshiped at the high places, as the author notes in 3:2 that they had been doing previously. If your language has different words for “finished” and “completed” that would convey these different senses, it would be appropriate to use them in your translation.

26.note: The author is using the term **lip** to mean the shore of the **Sea of Reeds**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [on the shore of]

27.note: The author is using this possessive form to describe **men** who had expertise in sailing **ships**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [sailors]

28.note: In a context such as this, your language might say “went” instead of **came**. Alternate translation: [And they went]
See how you decided to represent the expression “120 kikkars” in 9:14.
